stories.headline: Messi up for record 3rd MLS MVP award; Sullivan, 17, gets historic nomination
stories.summary: Lionel Messi has been named a finalist for the 2026 MLS MVP award, as he seeks to become the first player to win the prize on three consecutive occasions.
stories.body:
Lionel Messi has been named a finalist for the 2026 Major League Soccer MVP award, as the Inter Miami captain seeks to become the first player to win the prize on three consecutive occasions.

Messi won the MVP award in 2024 and 2025, becoming the second player to ever win the trophy twice, alongside Preki (Predrag Radosavljević), who won the title in 1997 and 2003.

- Will MLS teams' regular-season momentum last the two weeks before the playoffs start?

- Every eliminated MLS team: What worked and what didn't in 2026, what needs improving in 2027?

- Brotherly love: Cavan, Quinn Sullivan both score as Philly soars into playoffs

Eight-time Ballon d'Or winner Messi already clinched a record second straight Golden Boot award after scoring 26 goals in the 2026 regular season.

Messi joins finalists Evander (FC Cincinnati), Guilherme (Houston Dynamo FC) Hany Mukhtar (Nashville SC), and Cavan Sullivan (Philadelphia Union) for the award, which is named after former U.S. men's national team great Landon Donovan.

At 17 years old, Sullivan stands as the youngest player in MLS history to be named a finalist for the MVP award. He is also a finalist for the MLS Young Player of the Year award.

Last month, Sullivan became the youngest goalscorer in USMNT history when he found the net against Mexico.

MVP candidate Guilherme was named a finalist for the MLS Newcomer of the Year award, alongside Antoine Griezmann (Orlando City SC). Guilherme recorded 16 goals and 10 assists, while Griezmann managed 14 goals and eight assists.

Griezmann earns the recognition after joining Orlando City in July after finishing the 2025-26 season with Atlético Madrid in Spain.

Finalists for each end-of-the-year award received the highest average in votes from MLS club technical staff, MLS first-team players and select media members. Each group accounted for 33.3% of the overall results, according to MLS.

Winners will be announced during the 2026 playoffs, which begin on Nov. 19.

stories.headline: 76ers Joel Embiid (foot) questionable, LeBron James (back) out vs. Raptors
stories.summary: 76ers center Joel Embiid is questionable for Thursday night's game against the Raptors with right foot plantar fascia management. LeBron James is out with lower back/sciatica management.
stories.body:
PHILADELPHIA -- Philadelphia 76ers center Joel Embiid, who is questionable for Thursday night's game against the Toronto Raptors with right foot plantar fascia management, said he has "no idea" if he'll play.

"We'll see what they have to say and then we'll go from there," Embiid said, referring to the Sixers' medical staff.

LeBron James, who was ruled out with lower back/sciatica management, was among the last players on the floor after shootaround, taking free throws.

James, who turns 42 next month, will now have four to five days off before he plays again. The Sixers are off Friday and Saturday. They have back-to-back games Sunday and Monday. James typically does not play in least one game of a back-to-back set so he could return Sunday against Indiana or Monday at Brooklyn.

James has averaged 15.1 points, 7.2 rebounds and 6.5 assists in 10 games for the Sixers this season.

Embiid has missed two games this season to manage his fascia injury, and the Sixers are 1-1 in his absence.

The Sixers would be significantly shorthanded in the frontcourt if Embiid is out. Big man Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain) and Dominick Barlow (back) have already been ruled out.

On this new-look Sixers team, Embiid has struggled the most to look like himself. He's begun this season with averages in points (17.7) and three-point percentage (12.1%) that would be career lows.

"I just haven't been aggressive," he said Thursday. "So I think it's on me to just be aggressive about making plays, whether it's making plays for someone else."

Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

stories.headline: MMA stars Merab Dvalishvili, Usman Nurmagomedov brawl at hotel in Abu Dhabi
stories.summary: MMA stars Merab Dvalishvili and Usman Nurmagomedov got into a public brawl at a hotel in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday.
stories.body:
Former UFC bantamweight champion Merab Dvalishvili and PFL lightweight champion Usman Nurmagomedov were involved in a physical altercation Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, with video of the incident widely circulated on social media.

Dvalishvili, who is in Abu Dhabi ahead of Saturday's Real American Freestyle event, posted a video of his bloodied face after the scuffle. Multiple videos of the incident showed Nurmagomedov, whose older brother, Umar, lost a bantamweight title fight to Dvalishvili in 2025, approach Dvalishvili from behind and slap him in the face.

Former UFC lightweight champion Ilia Topuria, who is friends with Dvalishvili, shared video of the encounter online. Following the initial slap, Dvalishvili attempts to go after Nurmagomedov. A chaotic scene quickly unfolded, involving multiple members from the camps of both fighters. In his video afterward, Dvalishvili refers to Nurmagomedov and his camp as "snakes."

"What a sneaky way, guys," Dvalishvili says. "What kind of fighters you guys are? What kind of man does this? If you want to try, let's do it the real way."

Abu Dhabi Police issued a statement Thursday, saying eight people were arrested for their part in the brawl, though they did not name Dvalishvili and Nurmagomedov specifically. Additionally, two people who filmed the encounter were also taken arrested. It is not clear whether any or all of the detained parties remain in custody.

Wednesday's confrontation marks the latest in a long-running feud between Dvalishvili and the Nurmagomedov team. Before his win over Umar in January 2025, Dvalishvili referred to Umar as "spoiled" and accused the Dagestani of being disrespectful. The two camps were involved in a brief altercation in July at another RAF event in Georgia.

Both Merab and Umar are scheduled to compete at RAF on Saturday. Dvalishvili faces former UFC title challenger Marlon Moraes, while Nurmagomedov will wrestle former UFC champion Urijah Faber.

Usman Nurmagomedov is currently in a state of restricted free agency, with much speculation whether he will leave the PFL to fight in the UFC in 2027.

stories.headline: Paul Scholes: Mauricio Pochettino has the 'presence' to be Man United boss
stories.summary: Paul Scholes believes Mauricio Pochettino is the right man to take over at Manchester United but is concerned they may have missed out on his best years
stories.body:
Paul Scholes believes Mauricio Pochettino is the right man to take over at Manchester United but is concerned they may have missed out on his best years.

Michael Carrick was sacked by United after winning just three of his 15 games in charge this season -- United's worst start to a domestic campaign since 1986.

Carrick took charge of training on Tuesday and Wednesday following the club's dramatic come-from-behind 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday but was finally relieved of his duties on Thursday.

Manchester United are now looking to appoint former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino, who is currently head coach of the United States, to succeed Carrick.

Pochettino guided Tottenham to a Champions League final in 2019 and took over at Paris St-Germain where he won the league and cup, but former United midfielder Scholes thinks United may have left it too late to appoint the Argentine.

He told The Good, The Bad and The Football podcast: "I think he's got the presence to manage a big football club like Manchester United. My only slight concern is they have come a little bit too late to the party.

"Mauricio Pochettino is a great manager. I just have that slight concern that we're not getting his best years.

"He's got a bit of a reputation of being a bridesmaid, not winning that many trophies. That possibly put Man Utd off a little bit in the past. They are in a totally different position now."

Pochettino's could be in charge for Manchester United's first game following the international break when they travel to Anfield to face rivals Liverpool next Sunday.

Nicky Butt believes the 54-year-old will have to get some players out of the squad in the January transfer window.

He added: "He's got to work out the ones he can trust, the ones he can't and quickly and get them out in January, he can't stick with that team until next season.

"Manchester United are that low down, they don't even need to think about winning anything at the minute."

Carrick led United to a third place finish last season having stepped in following Ruben Amorim's January exit and was rewarded with a two-year deal.

But Scholes believes he should never have got the job.

- Man United hope to seal Mauricio Pochettino deal on Thursday - sources

- Michael Carrick's Man United collapse: The stats behind his sacking

- Gary Neville slams Man United's 'classless' handling of Michael Carrick sacking

He said: "You've got to feel for Michael, Michael's not stupid. He knows winning one game out your first 10 league games is just not going to cut it.

"Interim seemed to suit him. Michael never really had the body of work as a manager behind him to manage a club like Manchester United."

Gary Neville said he also wished Carrick had not been handed the full-time role in the summer.

He said on Sky Sports: "Sad that it's come to this.

"I wish he hadn't got the job at the end of the season. I think at that time, I'd pretty much said that I felt this could happen.

"I didn't expect it to happen this quickly, but it is what it is. The position in the league is terrible. Inevitable that the decision had to be made."

stories.headline: How Cubs' Pete-Crow Armstrong became runaway NL MVP favorite
stories.summary: The Cubs' star center fielder hit another level midway through the 2026 season. Here's what shaped PCA's superstar turn.
stories.body:
It's easy to forget that Pete Crow-Armstrong was having a quiet first six weeks of the 2026 MLB season after signing a six-year, $115 million contract extension a few months earlier. The moment that turned the Chicago Cubs center fielder into a runaway favorite for National League MVP honors didn't come until mid-May -- in a matchup against the Atlanta Braves and 2024 Cy Young winner Chris Sale.

Crow-Armstrong's defense, as usual, had been outstanding. But while batting ninth in the order during the early portion of the year, he had yet to find his groove at the plate and was batting just .238 with a .679 OPS.

Cubs hitting coach John Mallee attempted a "we have nothing to lose moment" against the nasty left-hander. The Cubs decided to move the lefty-hitting Crow-Armstrong closer to the plate.

"You're either going to get hit or the ball's going forward," Mallee recalled saying to Crow-Armstrong going into the game. "There's only two options because you're standing on top of the plate now."

It was similar to what former Cubs star Anthony Rizzo tried years earlier under Mallee's tutelage. Back then, when Mallee expressed concern for Rizzo's health -- as his hit by pitch totals increased -- the former All-Star first baseman famously reminded Mallee that he had survived cancer so he wasn't much afraid of a baseball. Crow-Armstrong decided he was up for the challenge after talking to Rizzo about it. He wanted to get on base more. Getting hit was one way.

Crow-Armstrong didn't get hit, but he did go 1-for-2 off Sale that day. He turned on a 97 mph pitch for a single in the second then grounded out on a 3-1 count in the fifth. They were not headline generating plays, but they were the genesis for the months filled with such moments ahead.

"All of a sudden he started to narrow down against lefties," Mallee explained. "Then when we got him into the leadoff spot. I think he felt more involved in the offense. He was more into it and that's Pete. He's so competitive. When the s--- hits the fan, he wants to be in the fight. He ain't the guy on the sidelines."

'It's like a light switch went on'

Crow-Armstrong had made a commitment to getting on base more months before facing Sale and then getting moved to the top of the order. As one of the faster players in the league, he knew he couldn't use his speed if he wasn't making contact. His 41.7% chase rate in 2025 had to come down. He said as much in spring training -- but finding plate discipline as a free-swinging player is a delicate balance.

"It started with just learning how to evaluate his misses," Mallee said.

The Cubs hitting coach challenged Crow-Armstrong with a tactic that, in theory, takes chasing out of the equation before a hitter even steps into the batter's box. He told him to stay on the fastball and make the pitcher throw three strikes with his breaking stuff.

Mallee said Crow-Armstrong took to it "immediately," and Mallee noticed his newfound discipline at the plate.

"Wait a minute, he used to swing at those," Mallee thought at the time.

The walks started to come. In March and April 2025, Crow-Armstrong took six free passes. In 2026 during that timeframe, that climbed to nine, including four in the final six games of April. "Then we started putting pitchers in buckets," Mallee explained. "Lefties that throw from angles, guys that throw straight over the top, guys that have high, riding four-seams. So we tried to bucket these guys and then he remembered the approach he took off of that type of pitcher, maybe not that same guy, but that type of pitcher.

"It's like a light switch went on and he changed into a different person."

'He's like a piece of clay'

Crow-Armstrong didn't earn his first MVP award solely because of plate discipline, but his willingness to lay off bad pitches meant eventually he would see more good ones. That would lead to more damage.

In that vein, the wiry 24-year-old always displayed more power than his frame would suggest as it wasn't pure muscle that led him to 45 home runs. His coaches often describe him as "twitchy" at the plate with a natural ability to pull the ball in the air.

But timing was an issue at the beginning of the season. In the first 31 days of the season -- March 26 to April 27 -- Crow-Armstrong hit just one home run. He and Mallee huddled on it and decided a previous leg kick, which had been removed from his approach, might be an option to get him "started earlier." So they added that back in mid-May, right around the time of that game against Sale and the Braves. Mallee wanted him on the move in the box sooner to get his timing down. The leg kick worked in a big way.

"All of a sudden, his center of mass was moving sooner forward -- and much slower -- rather than shorter and later," Mallee explained. "That was a huge deal."

Crow-Armstrong also lowered his back elbow during drills to eliminate some slack in his swing.

"He said, 'I'm rolling with it,'" Mallee recalled. "And he took it right into the game. Right from the cage that day, right into the game, and then never looked back."

The results of all of it -- the plate discipline and the mechanical changes -- were immediate and lasting. In 119 games from the Chris Sale matchup to the end of the season, Crow-Armstrong slashed .294/.393/.638 which included 41 home runs, 31 stolen bases and 70 walks. His MVP season took shape.

"You just throw all these ideas at Pete, and then he's so athletic, he's like a piece of clay," Mallee said. "You just tell him to do something and he does it. Athleticism controls your body and space, right?"

But that doesn't mean Crow-Armstrong isn't working on his skills. Far from it. His work in the cage during the season is matched only by his offseason routine.

'There is no one more focused than him inside the gym'

Kyle Henmi has trained Crow-Armstrong since 2020, the year he was drafted. As the founder of Dawg Pound Athletics, which is located in the Los Angeles area, he has worked closely with the soon-to-be crowned MVP, understanding early on he had a special athlete.

"The first time I met him, I remember we were doing box jumps," Henmi recalled in a phone interview. "And I set up the box 24 inches, a standard height to start warming up with. And he did his first jump and this dude just floated all the way up to the top.

"I took a step back and I was like, 'What the ...' I was like, wow, that's a little different."

And so began their current seven-year relationship. Henmi has been part and parcel to Crow-Armstrong's development off the field, citing him as one of the hardest workers he has ever trained. Most great athletes he has worked with share the two gifts: natural ability and work ethic. Henmi says Crow-Armstrong "got after it" right away.

"He is fiery," Henmi said. "He will get on people's asses. He'll push people. He wants to be pushed. He likes to be yelled at. He's always screaming at the gym, 'Come on, motherf‐‐‐er motherf---er let's go.' And then we're throwing med balls at each other like, 'Hit me harder. That's all you got?'"

That description fits Crow-Armstrong's on-field demeanor as well -- though he has reeled in some of that instant aggression he feels after a negative moment. Throwing bats and helmets were more the exception than the norm this season -- a reverse from the past.

Mallee called it the "sixth tool," learning the mental side of the game. Crow-Armstrong himself has spoken often about not needing to be "on" every minute of the game. To let his mind relax when it's warranted.

Henmi describes a similar situation in workouts -- from chitchat about plans that night to intense, focused training. Mostly, that inherent aggression Crow-Armstrong feels is rewarded in the gym as it pushes him to the limits.

"There is no one more focused than him inside the gym," Henmi said. "It's an amazing thing to coach him because when I'm going over exercises, I can look into his eyes and he's literally just eyeballing every little minute detail that I'm doing and talking about."

Henmi's goal for Crow-Armstrong was never to bulk him up. At 6-foot, 184 pounds, what he lacks in muscle, he makes up for in "rotational force," according to the trainer. That's where his power comes from. Beginning in the minor leagues, Crow-Armstrong kept flashing his home run potential, but it emerged in a big way in 2025 when he hit 31 home runs before blasting past that total this year.

"I need to make you strong, but I don't need to make you as strong as someone like Shohei [Ohtani] or Pete Alonso or someone like that," Henmi explained. "I need you to be strong enough, but I want to keep doing all the jumping, all the plyometrics. I want to keep you snappy."

Henmi admits to getting "choked" up discussing his most prominent client. The duo began a journey that neither could have imagined would end with a surprising, runaway win for league MVP in just his second full season in the big leagues -- or perhaps one of them did imagine it.

"I remember him talking to me one day at the gym about him being a Hall of Famer," Henmi recalled. "And you can hear guys talk about themselves like that, but there was something different when he said that to me about how in 20 years when I'm in the Hall of Fame. And you could hear it in his voice, he truly means that.

"And he truly knows that if he continues to work hard, if he continues to stay humble, if he continues to do what he's doing, nothing's going to stop him."

stories.headline: Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad to continue at Racing Bulls for 2027
stories.summary: Liam Lawson will stay in Formula 1 alongside teammate Arvid Lindblad at Racing Bulls in 2027, ending weeks of speculation about the New Zealander's future.
stories.body:
Liam Lawson will stay in Formula 1 alongside teammate Arvid Lindblad at Racing Bulls in 2027, ending weeks of speculation about the New Zealander's future.

Lawson's place at the team had been under scrutiny in recent weeks, with Red Bull's Bulgarian junior Nikola Tsolov waiting in the wings.

Racing Bulls ended any doubt on Thursday, confirming Lawson and Lindblad will continue together for another year.

Lawson has been one of the year's standout performers, sitting ninth with 89 points, a run of form which continued with a strong showing at last weekend's São Paulo Grand Prix, where he started third and finished seventh. Rookie teammate Lindblad is 11th with 38.

Racing Bulls is fighting for fifth in the constructors' championship.

- Qatar, Abu Dhabi races set to go ahead as F1 rules out Imola backup plan for finale

- Lewis Hamilton visits Gaza border, urges Israel to 'let the aid trucks in'

Team boss Alan Permane, who last week signed a deal to stay in his role until 2029, said Lawson and Lindblad is the strongest lineup the team could ask for.

"We're delighted to be continuing with Liam and Arvid for 2027," Permane said. "Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we've seen the progress they've made, both individually and as a pairing. I have no doubt that this is the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition.

"Together, we have a solid foundation to build on the progress made this year, continue pushing ourselves forward and take the next step towards achieving our ambitions in 2027."

Red Bull has confirmed Tsolov as reserve driver for Red Bull and Racing Bulls in 2027. The 19-year-old currently competes in Formula 2 for Campos Racing and is second in the title standings with two races remaining.

The team are promising an "extensive" programme of free practice sessions and Testing of Previous Car running as allowed under the F1 rulebook.

Tsolov said: "I'm incredibly happy and grateful to Red Bull for giving me this opportunity. Since joining the Junior Team, I've received amazing support and have developed so much, both as a driver and as a person. My career has progressed incredibly quickly, and I owe a lot to everyone who has believed in me and helped me get to this point.

"My ambition is clear: I want to become an F1 driver. Having the opportunity to spend next year preparing for that next step is incredibly exciting. I'm confident that with the Team's support and experience, I'll have the best possible preparation to make sure I'm fully ready to take the next step onto the F1 grid when the time comes."

stories.headline: Despite injury and illness, Gus Teixeira is still one of this year's top prospects
stories.summary: Gus Teixeira spent much of his top-age year battling injury and illness, but still found a way to be in contention to be the top pick in the open pool, writes Japser Chellappah.
stories.body:
Gustavo Teixeira had a brilliant top-age campaign. He's worked his way into pick 1 conversations, and is locked into the first handful of selections on draft night.

His success is made all the more impressive considering what's played out behind the scenes.

"I had the ankle injury at the start of the year in the first praccy game," Teixeira tells ESPN.

"It was kind of a bit annoying because every week I thought I'd be playing but it just got pushed back. I had the calf injury, I was out for five or six weeks. I rehabbed that, played a game and then the foot pulled up sore and that's why I'm not testing [at the AFL Draft combine].

"I've also been sick for basically the whole year with a virus."

Teixeira, a powerful forward-half midfielder, played valiantly through glandular fever-like symptoms that didn't get diagnosed until the conclusion of the National Championships.

He was playing games deep in the forward 50 but still finding himself short of breath and unable to hit top gear. After being diagnosed with a severe iron deficiency and receiving an infusion he felt the energy he'd been lacking return, but not before a calf injury linked to his virus took Teixeira out for all but one game in the back half of the season.

Most top-10 chances at the AFL Draft thrive off injury-free seasons where they can continually put their name up in lights. Teixeira couldn't do that this year, so he made his moments count.

His first game back from an ankle concern was in a Vic Metro trial game where he showed his worth, kicking two goals from 20 disposals in a best afield display.

"It was a good day out, I was pretty happy with that. It was annoying I couldn't do a bit more of that throughout the year but I'm sure I can do that in the future."

Teixeira had locked himself into Metro's National Championships outfit by halftime, showing off the power and class that recruiters covet.

At the National Championships he was playing under duress from his undiagnosed virus, but he still took the opportunity to show his value deep in attack.

"Obviously I was sick so I was resting a bit, I was sore the first week and they wanted me to play more forward. I kicked a few goals and they wanted me to stay down forward and that's where I was able to impact the most," he tells ESPN.

Teixeira claimed All-Australian honours, booting seven goals in his four outings including a best on ground demolition of the Allies where he kicked four goals from 22 touches.

It was an element of his game that proved his worth outside of the centre square. Teixeira got to dangerous spots and created separation with proactive running, and from there was able to demonstrate his cleanliness and class to make his chances count.

"I've always thought I want to be a midfielder, I want to play in there. Skills are very important as a midfielder so you've got to be clean and you've got to be able to kick. I'm just chipping away at it and improving."

Teixeira is of Brazilian descent via his father Matt, who was born in the city of Belo Horizonte before moving to Australia when he was 25.

He brings Gus back to Brazil every year, and that connection to a non-English speaking country would allow Teixeira to join zoned club St Kilda's Next Generation Academy if not for friction points within the AFL's own NGA rules.

"Belo Horizonte is just inland of Rio... It's like the size of Melbourne but no one's really heard of it. It's a fully different culture and it's always great to go back," he explains.

"The AFL changed the rules for the regions this year, so they allow South American people this year but you need to be in it for three years. I would've only been in it for a year... my younger siblings are in it now. I've got a brother, Eddie, who's 12 and my sister Lucy who's 14."

Like a host of the top prospects this year, Teixeira has been an Essendon supporter his whole life. The Bombers have the top pick and Teixeira is within that bracket of the pool.

"I haven't thought about the Bombers pick-wise, but just the club and thinking about what it would be like obviously going to the Bombers, it'd be great at the moment. They're getting in some good coaches and they've got some good players coming through.

"Really though I'd be stoked to get drafted to any club, moving interstate would be a pretty cool experience. I'm always trying to get the best out of myself, I've always tried to be the best at everything and just put my best foot forward so I'll do that anywhere."

stories.headline: Dirk Kuyt leaves Fenerbahce a week after defeating Liverpool
stories.summary: Dirk Kuyt left Fenerbahce on Wednesday, one week after guiding the team as interim coach to beat his old club Liverpool in the Champions League.
stories.body:
ISTANBUL -- Dirk Kuyt left Fenerbahce on Wednesday, one week after guiding the team as interim coach to beat his old club Liverpool in the Champions League.

The former Netherlands forward took charge of that 3-2 win in Istanbul despite the club already having made a deal with Emre Belözoğlu to take over.

Kuyt returned in July to Fenerbahce, where he played from 2012-15, to assist coach Ismail Kartal who resigned last month.

"We thank you from the bottom of our hearts for all that you have contributed to these colors," Fenerbahce said in a social media post announcing Kuyt's exit. "Today we say goodbye to you but your place in this big family will never change."

Belözoğlu, a former captain of the club, takes over a team sixth in the Turkish league and 19th in the 36-team Champions League standings.

Fenerbahce's next Champions League opponent is Shakhtar Donetsk in London on Nov. 25.

stories.headline: Wings' Paige Bueckers, Azzi Fudd talk relationship on pod
stories.summary: Azzi Fudd hosted Wings teammate Paige Bueckers on her podcast and the two discussed their relationship, Dallas' season and Fudd's recovery from knee surgery.
stories.body:
Dallas Wings teammates Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers, the past two WNBA No. 1 draft picks, spoke on Fudd's podcast Friday about a variety of topics, including a personal life update.

"We're not together anymore; it's been a while," Bueckers said on the "Fudd Around and Find Out" podcast. "[We] share that because everybody [was] like, 'Oh my gosh, they're teammates, how is this going to work?'"

Bueckers and Fudd, who were teammates in college at UConn, said they felt the need to address their relationship status in part because of allegations it factored into the Wings picking Fudd at No. 1 in April. Fudd was chosen over TCU guard Olivia Miles, who went on to be the Rookie of the Year for the Minnesota Lynx. Spain's Awa Fam (Seattle Storm) was taken third, followed by teammates from the 2026 champion UCLA Bruins: Lauren Betts (Washington Mystics), Gabriela Jaquez (Chicago Sky) and Kiki Rice (Toronto Tempo).

Fudd, Fam, Betts and Miles were all No. 1 at different points in ESPN's mock draft in the months before the April draft. Bueckers said her previous relationship with Fudd had no impact on Dallas' decision.

"We were not together before she got drafted," Bueckers said. "She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it. She's an amazing human, an amazing basketball player. And we're still friends, we're still cool.

"We played an entire season together; we're the utmost professionals."

Fudd averaged 13.1 points but was limited to just 30 games after an injury to her right knee led to season-ending arthroscopic surgery in August. She offered an update on her health.

"My offseason's been good," Fudd said. "Lots of rehab, lots of training, lots of on-court workouts, lots of traveling. It's been busy.

"I think there's a lot I can improve on. Especially the iso game; I feel like I'm not too comfortable with that yet. I know I'm capable of doing a little bit more. Watching someone like Paige who is able to create from anywhere ... that's great inspiration for me."

Bueckers averaged 20.9 points, 4.1 rebounds and 5.9 assists, and was named to the All-WNBA second team as Dallas reached the playoffs as the No. 7 seed.

The Wings were eliminated in the first round by the eventual champion Golden State Valkyries. Bueckers said she learned a lot from her first playoff experience and complimented Golden State.

"The Valkyries' defense, I can't explain to you how tough they are," Bueckers said. "They swarm, they send bodies, they trap you, they blitz you, they're so connected. I'm glad I got to have that experience against them to open my eyes to what the playoffs are like -- the physicality, the pressure, the environment.

"And I'm proud of our season. I hated losing; I sat and was pissed about it for like a week. I reached out to [Sue Bird] about it, what was her first playoff experience like. I didn't play as well as I wanted to. But it was my first experience, going against a really good opponent, and I was learning and growing through it all."

Fudd and Bueckers also addressed the Wings' move to the 19,000-seat American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas next season after playing at UT Arlington's College Park Center, which seats over 7,000, since the franchise relocated to Texas in 2016.

"UTA was a vibe; we had a ball, we did our thing there," Bueckers said. "But definitely excited to move into Dallas. New times."

While the change in venue will lead to more eyes on Wings games, the two players said they're hoping for less scrutiny of any on-court behavior.

Both said fans shouldn't read into interactions the two have with each other or their teammates as anything other than normal team behavior. They also said they don't stand for "hate of any kind" or "tearing people down to lift us up."

"We've seen a lot of negativity," Bueckers said. "We've had stuff sent to us, stuff sent to our family, our friends. There's been some crazy things said about us. We still support each other, we're still going to be great friends, we're still going to be great teammates. All the negative things can be put aside, and you don't need to overanalyze everything."

Fudd added with a chuckle, "Also, we don't need messages [from fans] on what the other person's doing. We've addressed everything we need to, and the rest will stay with us."

stories.headline: Subtle reason Jillaroo will cause Cup final headaches
stories.summary: Jillaroos fullback Tamika Upton has explained why Jesse Southwell commanded selection for the World Cup final against New Zealand.
stories.body:
The numbers are impressive, but it's what doesn't show up on the stats sheet that Tamika Upton likes most about Jesse Southwell.

The Brisbane five-eighth won a tight selection battle to replace Sydney Roosters premiership winner Jocelyn Kelleher for Sunday's Women's World Cup final.

Kelleher started in three of Australia's four Cup games and was player of the match in the 40-0 win over Samoa on Test debut.

Southwell, who will partner Tarryn Aiken in the halves, filled her boots with 44 points of her own in the record-breaking 124-6 win over Wales.

Kelleher kicks goals too and shared a strong bond with Roosters teammate and halfback Aiken during their NRLW title win, but has been named in the 21 jersey for the clash with New Zealand.

"Tarryn and Jesse haven't played too much footy together, but I've been fortunate to play a lot with the both of them and watching them both link up is going to be pretty special," Australia and Brisbane fullback Upton said.

"The best thing about Jesse, and this goes unnoticed and without stats, is how much space she creates for the people outside of her.

"I've been fortunate enough to have that pretty much my whole career, and I'm excited for her to do that for Taryn and make her job a little bit easier.

"She's young, she's energetic, she's enthusiastic, she wants the ball and she wants to be a part of the game."

Australia cruised into the final four before receiving a welcome test in their comeback semi-final defeat of Fiji.

"The record-breaking games are probably not the best when you're prepping for finals footy, which is so different," Upton said.

"We've had the luxury of everything working out for us and that just doesn't happen when it comes to finals.

"So it was good to be under the pump."

stories.headline: Will MLS teams' regular-season momentum last the two weeks before the playoffs start?
stories.summary: The MLS regular season ended on Saturday, but it will be nearly two weeks before the playoffs begin. It's a long time for a hot team to cool off.
stories.body:
With MLS Cup playoffs approaching, one word that continually comes up is "momentum." Does a team have it? If so, how can it maintain it, especially against the league's better teams? If not, how can the team get it back?

That said, the postseason does plenty to wreck the very concept of momentum. The league's playoffs are as unpredictable as it gets. Brackets are routinely demolished.

Nobody knows better the fickle nature of momentum than former MLS player and current Apple TV broadcaster Dax McCarty. He was part of the 2013 Supporters' Shield-winning Red Bull New York side that was eliminated in the Eastern Conference semifinal by the Houston Dynamo, thanks in part to a red card in the first leg to standout defender Jamison Olave.

McCarty was also part of the 2024 Atlanta United side that squeaked into the playoffs on Decision Day, beat CF Montréal in the wild card and then sprung an incredible upset against the juggernaut that was that year's Inter Miami side in Round 1. The win over Miami was aided by Atlanta keeper Brad Guzan performing physics-defying feats of gymnastics in the Five Stripes' goal.

"If the playoffs have taught us anything over the course of Major League Soccer's existence, it's that [you should] throw all that stuff out the window at times," McCarty told ESPN. "Throw tactics out the window, throw out momentum, throw out form, because one crazy play, one red card, one fluky goal can be the difference between advancing or your season being over."

Yet momentum is something that is still prized by coaches. In a world of fine margins, if you believe that you're going to win because of how you're playing in the moment, then the chances are better that the form will continue.

"I think momentum always matters, whether it's going into the postseason or whether it's the second game of the season," Houston Dynamo manager Ben Olsen said. "I think it matters mostly just because you want your team peaking around playoff time, and being the best version of themselves."

San Jose Earthquakes boss Bruce Arena stressed that momentum is as much a state of mind as it is about results. That's especially true if a coach feels his team is still short of its best.

"It doesn't have to be a terrific run going into the playoffs, but you have to have a team going in with confidence," he said. "You need to have a pretty good idea about what your team's about and how you want to go about your business in the playoffs.

"Probably the psychological part of it is more important than actually the tactical part of it. You just got to get inside the team and make sure that they enter the game with the confidence that they can get a result."

That appears to be true for the Quakes, who finished the season by going 4W-7D-2L. Houston, who faces San Jose in the first round, went a more sobering 2W-7D-4L.

At this stage of the season, teams have already been together for 10 months, so a manager is bound to know what makes his team tick. That doesn't mean said manager's work is done. There could be collaborative meetings in terms of refining how the team wants to approach a certain opponent.

Individual meetings might be needed as well to bolster the confidence of a particular player. A lineup change or a subtle tactical tweak could help a team as well. Arena stressed there is no formula for how he handles things.

"I think I've been in seven MLS Cup finals and won five of them, and I don't think I can tell you that I had the same approach to any of them," Arena said. "Every one was different."

The issue of momentum -- whether trying to maintain it or generate it -- faces some tricky obstacles this postseason. Following last Saturday's Decision Day, the teams that qualified for the playoffs will get around two weeks between matches due to the FIFA international window.

With rhythm broken, the playing field would appear to be more level. That provokes myriad questions in terms of approach. McCarty said the break "absolutely" has an effect on rhythm, momentum and potential injuries.

"How hard do you push your players? You want your players in form, but you also don't want them to get injured," McCarty said. "How hard are the coaches going to push their players?"

There seem to be two paths a manager can take. They either have a scrimmage against another MLS team, or they have an intra-squad match, albeit one in a stadium with referees, the better to simulate a real match. There are pros and cons to both. With injury prevention paramount, playing against another MLS team would appear to offer less control on the level of physicality.

"I think you would want to keep it in-house in terms of an intra-squad scrimmage to try to keep your players fit, to try to keep your players sharp, and with the very real caveat before the game to say, 'Listen, there are no dumb tackles. There are no slide tackles,'" McCarty said. "If you are an Inter Miami fan or a New England Revolution fan or a Nashville SC fan, you're telling young players that might be involved, 'You are not allowed to touch Hany Mukhtar. You're not allowed to touch Carles Gil. You're not allowed to touch [Lionel] Messi.'

"Those are the very clear expectations you have to set. But guess what? That doesn't actually give you a realistic playoff feel. It's whoever can find the right balance, whoever can be at their sharpest and fittest going into these first rounds of games, is going to like their chances."

Olsen indicated he wasn't particularly worried about dealing with the break, although he declined to specify which kind of scrimmage he would utilize. His thinking is that he's dealt with bye weeks so many times over the years that, "We all have a recipe for that."

Sure, he might change a few things here and there, but the concepts remain consistent, and he trusts his sports science department to get things right.

"There's a physical periodization, and there will be a tactical periodization from our side, but it's one that again has been, we've delivered, I don't know, 10, 15 times in the last three and a half years," he said.

Olsen admitted, though, that this time there's a twist.

"You're coming out of this into the most important game of the year, and that's a little bit new," he said.

Arena said he'll be going the intra-squad scrimmage route, although the international window brings another wrinkle to his preparations. What kind of condition will his four players that go away for international duty be in when they get back is a giant unknown.

"If you have players getting called up for international duty, they're likely starters in your team as well," Arena said. "So there's a lot of challenging things for coaches and players as you enter the playoffs. And this year it's been even more complicated because of the international window and the poor planning on the part of Major League Soccer."

This much is clear. Every manager will be trying to build momentum, wherever they can find it.

stories.headline: Warriors' Stephen Curry out at least 2 weeks with oblique tear
stories.summary: Warriors star Stephen Curry has an oblique abdominal tear and will be reevaluated in two weeks.
stories.body:
HOUSTON -- Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry will miss at least two weeks after suffering an oblique abdominal tear, it was announced Thursday.

Curry exited Wednesday's loss to the Houston Rockets with 6:25 remaining in the first quarter and later had an MRI.

He started grabbing at his right side a few minutes into the game, attempting to play through the pain while sporadically looking over at the training staff. With 7:22 left in the first quarter, Curry came off a Draymond Green screen and nailed a 28-foot 3-pointer but yelled in pain after the release and signaled toward the bench.

Coach Steve Kerr said Curry told him the tweak of his side was an injury he hadn't felt before.

"Concern is high," Kerr said.

Curry will miss at least the next seven games against the San Antonio Spurs, New Orleans Pelicans, Dallas Mavericks, Memphis Grizzlies, Boston Celtics, Sacramento Kings and Portland Trail Blazers.

The Warriors (8-4) were down 19-10 when Curry exited, clawed back to tie it but ultimately lost by seven points, snapping an eight-game winning streak that had been spurred by a surging Curry, who is averaging 27.8 points in 26.3 minutes per game this season.

He also is shooting a career-high 45.7% from 3-point range this season.

At halftime, prior to leaving the arena for an MRI, Curry spoke to his teammates, told them to focus on the task at hand and assured them that he would get through this latest injury fine.

This is the latest blow to an already depleted Warriors team. Starting wings Jimmy Butler III and Moses Moody are out rehabbing long-term knee injuries. Projected starting center Kristaps Porzingis stepped away from the team and sport entirely. Backup guard Brandon Williams strained a hamstring and will miss at least a week.

The Warriors were 13-26 in the 39 games that Curry missed last season. This season, they are 1-1 without Curry, who also is averaging 3.9 assists and 3.7 rebounds.

"The spirit of this team is better," Green said. "We're more certain of who we are, what makes us a good team. I think that puts us in a better position to be successful without him as opposed to where we were last year. Then obviously [Yaxel Lendeborg], having a guy you can give the ball to and he can create an advantage. [Brandin Podziemski] is playing a lot better. ... It puts us in a better position."

stories.headline: UFC's Josh Hokit says he'll 'never' regret vulgar Michelle Obama remarks
stories.summary: UFC fighter Josh Hokit, who will challenger for the heavyweight title on Saturday, says he'll "never" regret his vulgar comments about former First Lady Michelle Obama,
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- UFC heavyweight Josh Hokit said he has no regrets about using the White House as a bully pulpit to make an extraordinary and unfounded attack based on a right-wing conspiracy theory about former first lady Michelle Obama.

Hokit made his vulgar remarks inside the Octagon in June after winning his fight at the UFC event to mark President Donald Trump's 80th birthday on the South Lawn of the White House.

Hokit fights for the first time since then on Saturday when he challenges heavyweight champion Ciryl Gane in the main event of UFC 334 at Madison Square Garden.

Hokit again made a series of crass insults about other fighters on the fight card on Wednesday inside a New York hotel before taking questions about his championship bout and his remarks on Obama.

"I'll never look back and be like, I regret that," Hokit said.

Wearing a black stocking cap over an American flag bandana, sunglasses and fight gloves, Hokit said he "took the rap of a villain" before he burst into what he called a freestyle rap to express his lack of regret.

Hokit said he was "sure it wasn't" the right thing to do to insult the former first lady but was proud the remarks had put his image on Trump's Truth Social posts. In one post, Hokit appeared in cartoon form alongside UFC chief Dana White in the White House briefing room.

Trump said over the weekend he had offered White the job of White House press secretary. White declined the frivolous offer.

"I'm here to take what's mine," Hokit said. "If I've got to rub some people the wrong way, if I've got to say some (stuff) in the wrong location, it is what it is. Was it not a good location to say it? I mean, we're at the White House. That house represents freedom of speech. So it is what it is. I think it was the perfect location to say it."

The 28-year-old Hokit is 10-0 in his MMA career and has won all six fights since joining UFC in 2025.

stories.headline: Reaction as Man United sack Michael Carrick as manager
stories.summary: Manchester United have sacked manager Michael Carrick after a poor run of results. Catch up on the latest reaction to the news.
stories.body:
Michael Carrick was sacked as Manchester United head coach on Thursday after the club dropped into the Premier League relegation zone (18th) with just one league win in 10 games (five draws, four losses) -- their worst-ever start to a league season.

A rollercoaster 4-4 draw was saved late at Old Trafford against Aston Villa at the weekend, and came after a 3-2 win from 2-0 down against Roma in the UEFA Champions League in midweek, but it was not enough to save Carrick from the sack.

United States coach Mauricio Pochettino is the favored candidate to replace Carrick, with the United hierarchy -- led by co-chairman Joel Glazer, minority owner Jim Ratcliffe, CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox -- assessing options in the coming days.

Catch up on the latest reaction to the news.

stories.headline: Who will win MVP? Picks, analysis for 2026 MLB awards week
stories.summary: Baseball's best players and managers of 2026 collect their hardware this week.
stories.body:
The baseball offseason has felt pretty normal so far if you can put the overhanging labor negotiations out of your mind. Some of that normalcy comes from the gradual easing into the initial phases of the hot stove season -- contract options, roster maneuvering, free agency filing -- that point toward next season.

That's administrative stuff, though, and not as fun as the parade in Milwaukee -- or this week, when MLB is handing out its major awards in what closes the books on the 2026 season.

This year's awards week added a new honor being handed out by the Baseball Writers' Association of America: the Reliever of the Year Award, which recognizes the top bullpen maestro from each league.

Here's how the rest of this week's schedule lays out:

Thursday: MVP (7 p.m. ET, MLB Network)

Below, we break down the major award winners so far -- and preview Thursday's grand finale.

Jump to an award:

MVP | Cy Young | Reliever of the Year

Rookie of the Year | Manager of the Year

Most Valuable Player

American League

Finalists:

Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros

Junior Caminero, Tampa Bay Rays

Bobby Witt Jr., Kansas City Royals

What to know: Here are the OPS+ figures for the qualifying hitters who ranked second through sixth in the AL: 153, 149, 148, 146 and 144. No. 1? That would be Alvarez ... at 190. He dominated the leaderboards for AL hitters at a Wilt Chamberlain-like level, sweeping all the slash categories and falling one homer and seven RBIs shy of a Triple Crown.

Alvarez made that production count, pacing AL hitters in win probability added (6.9), with a figure that was 68% better than the second-place finisher, Pete Alonso. At 81-81, Alvarez's Astros barely eked out a postseason spot. Without him, they would have been lottery-bound for sure.

Witt should remain a fixture in the finalist group for years to come. He was an easy pick once again this season even though, by his stratospheric standards, it wasn't his best year. He's just so good at so many things that the secondary parts of his game add elite value even when his batting line is more good than great.

AXE did not see Caminero as the third finalist, though it's hard to fault the voters for picking him. From a metrics standpoint, at least the ones that feed AXE, the issue was situational hitting. Caminero ranked fourth in the AL in batting runs above average, but just 12th in the win probability added by all that production.

Doolittle's pick: Alvarez

National League

Finalists:

Pete Crow-Armstrong, Chicago Cubs

Shohei Ohtani, Los Angeles Dodgers

Brice Turang, Milwaukee Brewers

What to know: AXE and the BBWAA were in lockstep when it came to identifying the finalists. And, really, the drama in this race was more or less over by the time we hit Labor Day. Crow-Armstrong just kept getting better and better while Ohtani struggled with injuries so nagging that he had little impact in October.

The trajectory of the race shows us how much of a tease it was for a few weeks there. After Ohtani built a huge and predictable lead early in the season, Crow-Armstrong took off in June (he posted a 1.249 OPS for the month) and just kept going. By the beginning of August, he had overtaken Ohtani in AXE, and with the Dodgers headed to Wrigley Field on Aug. 3, it felt like we were watching an epic head-to-head race that would be one for the history books.

It was, but only for Crow-Armstrong, who posted one of the best two-way seasons in baseball history. Well, make that three-way. In the subcategories of bWAR, PCA led the NL in both batting runs above average (44) and baserunning runs (9), and ranked third in fielding runs (16). That's how you end up with 9.8 bWAR -- the fourth-best total by a Cubs hitter in the franchise's 151-year history.

Ohtani's greatness is hardly diminished by his 2026 season. Look where he is on this leaderboard despite playing injured for much of the second half of the season. As for the often-overlooked Turang, he'll likely have to content himself with the championship ring he'll get when next season begins. It's a trade-off he'll be happy to make.

Doolittle's pick: Crow-Armstrong

Cy Young

American League

Winner: Cam Schlittler, New York Yankees

Final tally: Schlittler 210 (30 first-place votes, unanimous), Dylan Cease 110, Parker Messick 84, Drew Rasmussen 72, Sonny Gray 21, Reid Detmers 9, Cade Smith 2, Bryan Baker 1, Michael Wacha 1

Doolittle's pick: Schlittler

Takeaway: Schlittler is so implacable in his demeanor and so consistently elite with his results that it's really easy to forget that four years ago, he was an unheralded seventh-round draft pick out of Northeastern. Now he's a Cy Young winner and was a unanimous selection at that.

Schlittler's 7.0 bWAR as a second-year pitcher was historically significant, and not just in the context of the Yankees' celebrated annals. But contemporary usage limits make it hard to put that into eye-popping context, so I keep coming back to his 215 ERA+ -- the best in Yankees history. I've written that stat several times now but, come on, that's incredible.

Schlittler has never come close to failing at any point since he arrived in the majors. He has a 2.23 regular-season ERA, including a league-leading 1.95 mark this season. And he has been even better in the playoffs, with a 1.44 mark in four outings. He's the seventh Yankee to win the honor. The first six won it a single time as a Yankee. Schlittler has a great chance to become the first pinstriped pitcher to win it more than once.

National League

Winner: Jacob Misiorowski, Milwaukee Brewers

Final tally: Misiorowski 210 (30 first-place votes, unanimous), Cristopher Sanchez 99, Chris Sale 98, Yoshinobu Yamamoto 63, Jesus Luzardo 34, Mason Miller 4, Eduardo Rodriguez 2

Doolittle's pick: Misiorowski

Takeaway: I don't know what's going to become of Jacob Misiorowski's career, but he's a gift to the game in so many ways. And as much as I try to sidestep the slobbering over his velocity readings, I get why they attract so much attention. No starter has lit up the pitch trackers quite like he has.

But velocity by itself won't win you a Cy Young. One of the things that sets Misiorowski apart is that if he topped out at 97 mph, he'd still be a good pitcher. That might not have been the case a year ago, but his improvement in the finer points of command and consistency has flipped that in a stunning fashion. Misiorowski has become the full package, and he can become even better.

The other thing that sets Misiorowski apart is that he's a genuine character. He's that kid who comes over after school and plays video games with your son. He's Nuke LaLoosh from "Bull Durham" except he's really good. And he's the best pitcher on baseball's newest World Series championship club.

Will Misiorowski be throwing 105 mph in three years? I don't know. But what I strongly suspect is that as we try to recalibrate our standards as to what an elite starting pitcher looks like in the 2020s, we can start with what Misiorowski, Paul Skenes, Tarik Skubal, Schlittler and a handful of others are doing. And The Miz very much belongs in that group.

Reliever of the Year

American League

Winner: Louis Varland, Toronto Blue Jays

Final tally: Varland 146 (16 first-place votes), Cade Smith 133 (7), Bryan Baker 111 (6), Aroldis Chapman 36, Josh Hader 22 (1), David Bednar 20, Jacob Latz 17, Brent Headrick 12, Garrett Whitlock 6, Grant Taylor 3, Spencer Miles 2, Tyler Rogers 2

Doolittle's pick: Smith

Takeaway: This feels like minds were made up early in September, because while I had Varland as the winner for a big chunk of the season, I very much feel like Smith overtook him by season's end. Varland had that sparkling 1.27 ERA, but both pitchers gave up 20 runs this season. Smith had fewer that were unearned. Meanwhile, Smith led handily in win probability added and did so as a key cog on a playoff team. This was a miss by the voters, of which I was one, casting one in favor of Smith.

National League

Winner: Mason Miller, San Diego Padres

Final tally: Miller 210 (30 first-place votes), Jhoan Duran 110, Trevor Megill 66, Adrian Morejon 64, Raisel Iglesias 17, Mason Montgomery 11, Didier Fuentes 10, Tanner Scott 8, Aaron Ashby 6, Dylan Lee 3, Brandyn Garcia 2, Abner Uribe 2, Emilio Pagan 1

Doolittle's pick: Miller

Takeaway: An easy selection. There are a lot of ways to look at relief pitcher value, but Miller checks off every box. He's the best in the game and one of those rare closers who gives you a little tingle of excitement as soon as he's summoned from the bullpen. You want to know why Jackson Chourio's game-winning single against the Padres in the NLDS was one of the signature moments of the playoffs? Well, it was a really big hit, of course. But what made it transcendent is that he did against Miller. That tells you all you need to know.

Rookie of the Year

American League

Winner: Kevin McGonigle, Detroit Tigers

Final tally: McGonigle 204 (28 first-place votes), Parker Messick 122 (2), Payton Tolle 54, Munetaka Murakami 39, Carter Jensen 31, Chase DeLauter 23, Kazuma Okamoto 17, Tristan Peters 12, Sam Antonacci 2, Travis Bazzana 2, Walbert Urena 2, Dylan Beavers 1, Henry Bolte 1

Doolittle's pick: McGonigle

Takeaway: The cases for McGonigle and Guardians starter Messick were close by the numbers, so this seems to have come down to comparing an every-day player versus a starting pitcher. This result makes me wish we had separate rookie awards for hitters and pitchers, but I guess we already have plenty of awards.

McGonigle was a great pick, though, and I'm a little relieved that he didn't suffer in the voting because of his lack of big-time power numbers -- not that 18 homers for a 21-year-old middle infielder is pedestrian. But he added value in so many ways. According to Baseball Reference, McGonigle's final tally of 7.1 bWAR is the sixth best ever among AL position players.

That kind of performance demands recognition. McGonigle is the first Tiger to win Rookie of the Year since Michael Fulmer in 2016. As for Messick, his week isn't over: He's also a Cy Young finalist.

National League

Winner: Sal Stewart, Cincinnati Reds

Final tally: Stewart 170 (20 first-place votes), Carson Benge 107 (7), JJ Wetherholt 99 (3), Nolan McLean 70, TJ Rumfield 49, Logan Henderson 10, Bryce Eldridge 2, Didier Fuentes 2, A.J. Ewing 1

Doolittle's pick: Wetherholt

Takeaway: I thought we were past this kind of voting, which I hate to write because I don't like to rain on anybody's awards parade. Stewart is a fun player and a legit run producer, finishing with 32 homers and 112 RBIs. To be clear, Stewart is not just strictly an RBI compiler -- but this is a case where his difference in advanced metrics was just too much to overcome. Or at least it should have been.

Stewart seemed to be aware of this debate as he kind of made his own case during the pre-announcement interview, but it wasn't necessary. Stewart is the NL Rookie of the Year, and good for him. The last Red to win was Jonathan India in 2021.

Manager of the Year

American League

Winner: Will Venable, Chicago White Sox

Final tally: Venable 111 (15 first-place votes), Kevin Cash 98 (12), Chad Tracy 47 (3), Stephen Vogt 9, Aaron Boone 4, Joe Espada 1

Doolittle's pick: Venable

Takeaway: This is an award I'd never want to vote on. Sure, I have a system that rates managers, or rather, as I try to be transparent about, a system that seeks to measure factors that tend to correlate with Manager of the Year voting. Separately, I do think you can get a good feel for how a manager is impacting a specific team if you're around it a lot. But I'm able to reach that criteria with only a handful of managers in a given year. There is so much beyond data you need to know before you can really judge how a manager is doing.

I was exposed to Venable often this year, tracing back to spring training. It's always impossible to know how your judgment is impacted by results. A team going well invariably leaves a strong impression. One that isn't does not. That's natural.

With Venable, despite a couple of X's and O's mistakes, his connection to what was going on with a shockingly good White Sox team was apparent every step along the way. For a team that reached the playoffs, the White Sox turned over key roster spots consistently through the season, as an emerging ballclub should if it has the talent base to make it work. Through it all, the team and the roster always seemed like a cohesive continuation of what had already occurred.

Then came early August, roughly speaking, when it became apparent that Chicago did not have enough resources to run a starting rotation in a typical manner through the rest of the season. The acquisition of Luis Castillo not only did not fix that problem, it made it worse. The White Sox, with Venable leading the way, went into improv mode, appropriate for the city that gave the world Second City. Craft a pitching plan today and worry about tomorrow when it arrives. Venable and his collaborators made it work.

This year's White Sox had no business coming within one win of an ALCS appearance. It was too much, too soon. Yet that's exactly what happened. My metrics like Cash better, and he came close in the balloting. I love Cash as one of the two best managers in the game along with Pat Murphy. But anyone guiding a team that provided as much historical shock as did this year's White Sox demands recognition. Venable more than deserves this honor.

National League

Winner: Pat Murphy, Milwaukee Brewers

Final tally: Murphy 124 (20 first-place votes), Walt Weiss 86 (7), Don Mattingly 25 (1), Craig Stammen 24 (2), Dave Roberts 7, Craig Counsell 3, Don Kelly 1

Doolittle's pick: Murphy

Takeaway: It almost feels like Craig Counsell has become a villain in Murphy's story, which isn't at all fair. Yes, Counsell bolted, leaving his hometown team for a record contract with that club's chief rival. But come on, Counsell just became manager of the Cubs. It's not like he tied Bernie Brewer to some train tracks.

Still, for Wisconsinites who feed off schadenfreude, this is a sweet time, even better than a stop at Mars Cheese Castle just off I-94 south of Milwaukee. The manager in which you believed betrayed you for the one team you wouldn't want him to go to. His replacement, his mentor, the amiable but overlooked bench coach who is like a contemporary embodiment of Red Blow -- the bench coach for Pop Fisher in "The Natural" -- takes over. And in the first three seasons after that happens, he is named NL Manager of the Year. Also, lest we forget, in the third of those years, this grizzled coach gifts you the first World Series in franchise history.

The Brewers' title did not factor into the voting, but everything Pat Murphy did to put Milwaukee in position to achieve that title was already in place when the ballots were cast. Not the least of which was the 103 wins, a franchise record and far above where preseason forecasts had predicted the Brewers to be.

My metrics have loved Murphy all through his tenure, though it has to be acknowledged that part of the perception around the Brewers overachieving stems from the fact that they are chronically underrated. Still, come on. Has any team in recent times been more explained or defined by the personality of its manager and the standards that he demands his club meet?

One thing I loved about this season's great World Series matchup is that it was a clash between two managers who really mattered. And Murphy and Cash are very, very different in the way they go about it. That in itself says something positive about where the game of baseball is given this point in time and a testament to how managers, as much as ever, really matter.

stories.headline: Lewis Hamilton visits Gaza border, urges Israel to 'let the aid trucks in'
stories.summary: Lewis Hamilton urged Israel to let aid trucks into Gaza after visiting the Rafah border this week, adding in a passionate post "the past three years of Israel's genocide is appalling."
stories.body:
Lewis Hamilton urged Israel to let aid trucks into Gaza after visiting the Rafah border this week, adding in a passionate post "the past three years of Israel's genocide is appalling."

The seven-time world champion called for a "Free Palestine" during a news conference ahead of October's United States Grand Prix, and has previously called for a ceasefire in the region.

This week, Hamilton visited the Rafah crossing, the only land crossing between the Gaza Strip and Egypt and the hub of various humanitarian aid organizations.

After meeting aid workers and truck drivers on the ground, Hamilton posted a message about the trip to his 44 million Instagram followers.

"The past three years of Israel's genocide in Gaza is appalling," Hamilton wrote on Instagram. "It's an injustice for people to be denied their freedom, their safety and their dignity. No human being should be treated as though their life matters less."

Israel denies accusations of genocide, saying its military campaign in Gaza targets militants of terrorist group Hamas. Hamilton urged people not to ignore what is happening in the region.

"I know so many people that feel that same helplessness," he added. "That same need to do something rather than just watch. I don't want us to get used to their suffering. I don't want us to look away."

- Qatar, Abu Dhabi races set to go ahead as F1 rules out Imola backup plan for finale

Hamilton also met with North Sinai Governor Khaled Megawer.

The governor's office shared videos to its official Facebook page of Hamilton being briefed by Megawer on the aid coordination and the Ferrari driver greeting aid workers and inquiring how often they were able to enter Gaza through the Rafah crossing.

Last month, the World Health Organization (WHO) said repeated delays in bringing life-saving medicines, prosthetics and other supplies into Gaza can have "devastating consequences" for Palestinians who urgently need them.

Hamilton described seeing food trucks lined up and ready to go in, only to be delayed or not allowed in.

His post continued: "I saw walls stretching for miles, built to keep them in. Standing there, outside what felt like an open-air prison, all I could think about was getting in to help.

"At the Rafah border, I saw food trucks lined up ready to go, but they're regularly not allowed in or face major delays. The first driver in line that I spoke to had already been waiting over 12 hours. At the nearby logistics centre, I saw the hard work of the aid workers, but I also saw what gets rejected for crazy reasons. Sleeping bags, first aid kits, medical equipment, wheelchairs, even footballs for kids.

"Israel needs to fulfil its obligations under the ceasefire and let the aid trucks in. No excuse."

stories.summary: The 2026 AFL draft is rapidly approaching, so here's your guide for what to know, including key dates and times, players to know, academy-linked names, and every club's pick.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL Draft is fast approaching. Marvel Stadium will once more play host to the first round at 7:00pm AEDT on November 19, with the draft recommencing for the second round onwards on November 20.

Key dates and times
Where: Marvel Stadium

How to watch: Fox Footy

First round: Thursday, November 19, 7pm AEDT

Second round onwards: Friday, November 20, 7pm AEDT

Preseason and rookie draft: Monday, November 23, 3pm AEDT

Each club's picks

Adelaide: 15, 32, 35, 43, 54

Carlton: 13, 18, 31, 50, 59, 67, 73

St Kilda: 10, 16, 41

Sydney: 6, 38, 39, 47

West Coast: 3, 23, 56 (plus second round compensation pick)

Western Bulldogs: 42, 52, 53, 71

State of play and players to know
Essendon will be on the clock first, holding the top selection a decade on from the last time it took the number one pick to the AFL Draft. The Dons are expected to first bid on Port Adelaide-tied forward Dougie Cochrane, which will trigger a start-of-second-round compensation pick for the Bombers, Tigers and Eagles.

There are familial lines drawn throughout an exciting 2008-born cohort. Cody Walker is the son of high-flying Blue Andrew and will be headed to Princes Park. Cochrane is the son of former North Melbourne and Port Adelaide midfielder Stuart, though he isn't eligible to either team under the 100-game father-son rule. Instead, he's eligible to join the Power as part of their Next Generation Academy as an Indigenous prospect.

Top-10 riser Sam Gayfer is the nephew of 1990 premiership Pie Mick, and Koby LeCras brings goalkicking pedigree via 2018 premiership uncle Mark.

There will be up to five club-tied talents picked in the first round of the AFL Draft. But that won't necessarily result in an extended first night. Over the past five years the first round has averaged out to 25 selections accounting for father-son and academy bids, but clubs are expecting a number closer to the traditional 18 picks in the final intake of the 18-team competition.

Stricter stipulations around matching bids is at play, with clubs only able to use a maximum of two selections when matching for a club-tied prospect, meaning the selections of Port Adelaide, Carlton, Brisbane and GWS will be absorbed as early bids are matched.

We could see a record number of Indigenous talents picked in the first round. The high-water mark was four in 2005 and 2014, and all of Cochrane, Walker, Caylen Murray (Lions Academy), Toby Krasna and Jake Eime could be taken in the first round in 2026.

Thirteen of the top prospects have already been invited to Marvel Stadium on November 19.

Ethan Drever, Arki Butler and Heath Mellody are all still in contention to be the open pool No. 1 pick, with Harry Van Hattum, Gus Teixeira, Mitch Harris and Ethan Matthews (Giants Academy) rounding out the group on top of draft boards alongside Cochrane and Walker.

Murray, Gayfer, Wil Malady and Leo Steed have also received invites in a sign of club interest on night one.

Around 65 picks are expected to be taken across both nights which would surpass the 60 selections last year.
